title: When the Church Married the Power
subtitle: From Constantine to the modern fusion of faith and political power, the same trade keeps getting made. The church exchanges its prophetic distance for a seat at the table, and forgets it was sent to the table to tell the truth.
question: What happens to a church when it stops speaking truth to the powers and starts speaking on their behalf?
whyItMatters: There is a moment in the life of every church when power offers it something. Protection. Influence. A favorable ruler. A movement that promises to carry the faith into the halls where decisions are made. The offer always looks like an opportunity to do more good. It almost never looks like what it is, which is a transaction in which the church gives up the one thing only it can give, the freedom to say no to the powers, in exchange for the one thing the powers always have to give, proximity to themselves.
biblicalFoundation:
Jesus stood before Pilate, the man who held the machinery of Rome in the province, and said his kingdom was not of this world. He did not mean it was located somewhere else, off in the sky. He meant it did not run on the fuel that empires run on, which is force, fear, and the threat of the cross. A kingdom that came by Roman methods would not be his kingdom. It would be Rome with a new name.

This was the third temptation, the one in the wilderness where the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and offered them on a single condition. The kingdoms were real. The offer was real. There was a road to the rule of every nation, and it ran through one act of worship pointed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused the shortcut. He took the long road, the road that ended on a hill outside the city walls. The church has been offered that same shortcut in every century since, and has too often taken the bargain he turned down.

The prophets of Israel knew which side of the throne room they belonged on. Nathan walked into the king's house and said to David, 'You are the man.' Elijah stood in front of Ahab and named the thing. Amos confronted the religion of the comfortable and the politics of the powerful in the same breath. They did not serve the kings. They confronted them. The prophetic office was the office of distance, the voice that could only stay true if it stayed free.

The early church understood this in its bones because it had no other option. It met in homes. It buried its own. It refused the incense the empire asked for, the small pinch of worship that would have purchased peace, and it paid for that refusal in the arenas. It could not serve two masters, and it knew which one it had chosen, because the choice cost it everything Rome could take. The trouble began later, when Rome stopped killing the church and started funding it, and the church discovered that patronage is harder to refuse than persecution.
keyTexts: John 18:36, my kingdom is not of this world
Matthew 4:8-10, the third temptation, the kingdoms of the world offered by another road
2 Samuel 12:1-7, Nathan confronts David, you are the man
1 Kings 18:17-18, Elijah names the trouble of Israel to its king
Matthew 6:24, no one can serve two masters

churchRecord.led: The church has been at its truest when it had no power to protect and spoke anyway. The martyrs under Rome who would not burn the pinch of incense. The Confessing Church in Germany that signed the Barmen Declaration in 1934 and said the church has one Lord and it is not the Fuhrer, the church that sent Dietrich Bonhoeffer to a cell and a rope. The black church in the American South that held the moral center while the white church blessed the order around it. The Salvadoran priests and catechists who read the Gospel to the poor and were shot at the altar for it. In each case the church kept enough distance from power to tell it the truth, and in each case it paid.
churchRecord.failed: The church has been at its worst when power offered it a throne and it sat down. Constantine made the faith respectable in 313 and within a century the same church that had been fed to lions was sending heretics into exile by imperial decree. The Crusades baptized conquest and called the sword holy. The conquistadors carried the cross ahead of the chains. The German Christians draped the swastika over the altar and quoted Romans 13 to a regime building camps. The slaveholding pulpits of the American South found the Bible endlessly agreeable to the cotton economy. Every one of these was the same marriage, the church trading its prophetic distance for the protection and approval of the powers, and every one of them is our family record, not someone else's.

whereWeAgree: Almost every serious Christian, asked in the abstract, will say the church must keep enough distance from power to tell it the truth. The disagreement is never about the principle. It is about whose power we have gotten too close to, and we are always quicker to see the entanglement on the other side than the one we are standing inside.
captureLeft: On the left, the capture wears the language of justice and the church learns to baptize the progressive state. The faith becomes a chaplaincy to a political program, its prophets reduced to activists who never have a discouraging word for their own coalition. The kingdom of God gets quietly renamed as the platform, and any Christian who dissents from the platform is treated as having dissented from Christ. The state grows, the church applauds, and the prophetic voice goes silent in exactly the places the program has gone wrong, because you do not rebuke the king whose patronage you have learned to enjoy.
captureRight: On the right, the capture wears the flag and the church learns to fuse the Gospel with the nation. Faith becomes a tribal marker, a way of belonging to a people and a party rather than a way of belonging to Christ. The cross gets wrapped in the flag until no one can tell which one is being asked to save them. The church trades its prophetic distance for political access, for judges and influence and a strongman who promises to protect it, and in the trade it loses the freedom to say to that strongman the one word the prophets always kept in reserve, which is no. Power protected is the oldest idol in the book, and it does not stop being an idol because the cause is one we approve.
whereWeDiffer: Christians of good faith will disagree about how close is too close, and that range is legitimate. Some are called to run for office, to draft the law, to sit in the room where the budget is decided. Some are called to stand outside the room and name what is being done inside it. The faith does not require withdrawal from public life, and the demand that Christians stay out of politics is itself a kind of capture, the privatized faith the powers find most convenient. The difference that matters is not engagement versus withdrawal. It is whether the church has kept the freedom to tell its own side the truth, or whether it has sold that freedom for a seat.
theCost: The cost of distance is real and it should not be minimized. A church that will not be owned by either party will be useful to neither, and both will call it a traitor. It will lose its access, its favor, and a good portion of its congregation, the ones who came for the politics and stayed only as long as the church agreed with them. It will be lonely in an age that demands a side. But the cost of the marriage is higher, because a church wedded to power cannot speak truth to it, and a church that cannot speak truth to power has nothing left to say that the power could not have said for itself.
charge: Find the power you have stopped being able to criticize, and look hard at why. It will be the one you feel you must defend, the side you cannot bear to see indicted, the leader whose faults you have learned to explain. That is where the marriage already happened. I have my own, and naming yours will not absolve me of mine. The church does not lose its voice in one dramatic surrender. It loses it one comfortable silence at a time, and the silence always feels like loyalty while it is happening.
